newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovaks say critical U.S. envoy overstepped line. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Slovaks say critical U.S. envoy overstepped line. [CORRECTED 18:40 GMT]

text.p: A senior Slovak diplomat has accused the U.S. ambassador to Bratislava of over-stepping his competence by expressing concerns about Slovakia's commitment to the democratic basis of NATO membership.

Speaking in a weekend television debate aired on the private station Markiza, Jozef Sestak, secretary of state at the Foreign Ministry, said comments by Ambassador Ralph Johnson over sensitive criminal probes were inappropriate.
"We think that in some parts of his speech the ambassador mis-stepped and went beyond the line of what the ambassador of a state should do," Sestak said.

Last week, Johnson warned Bratislava that abandoning sensitive criminal probes linked by the opposition to a political feud between the president and the premier could damage Slovak ambitions of joining "western structures".
Michal Kovac Junior, adult son of President Michal Kovac, was kidnapped in August 1995 when he was bundled into the boot of his car and dumped outside a police station in Austria.

Two state detectives were sacked after saying their investigations led them to suspect the involvement of the state secret service (SIS) in Kovac Junior's abduction. A third investigator adjourned the case in May due to lack of evidence.

Former policeman Robert Remias was killed in a car blast this spring after acting as a contact with a former SIS member who has accused SIS chief Ivan Lexa of organising the abduction. Lexa is a close ally of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, who is locked in a bitter political feud with the president.
The police found that the blast had been caused by an unspecified explosive placed inside the car but later adjourned the case due to lack of evidence.

"We make no judgments about the outcome of these investigations, but abandoning them would in our view be very damaging to Slovakia's candidacy (to join western structures)," Johnson said in an address in Presov, eastern Slovakia.
Slovak Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik refused to comment on Johnson's remarks, saying he saw no reason to respond to one of the many ambassadors in Slovakia.

Sestak said, however: "I think he (Johnson) went too far because he commented on things which are unrelated to relations between the two states." (Corrects to make clear speaker was Sestak, not Hamzik).
In his televised comments, Sestak said that Johnson's words were all the more serious in that they came from the representative of the world superpower.
The Foreign Ministry had no immediate comment on Sestak's remarks.

In his speech Johnson also listed as examples of Slovakian foot-dragging on the path to democracy restrictive media laws, a law governing universities, and a language law widely seen as discriminatory against the country's large Hungarian minority.
On the same day as Johnson, another ambassador -- the EU's Georgios Zavvos -- also criticised Slovakian foot-dragging in implementing democratic reforms.

Slovakia insists that it should be in the first group of states to join the EU and NATO. But Brussels and Washington have more than once expressed concerns about Slovakia's democracy since populist premier Meciar was returned to power in 1994.
